classes.d: A bordered container for native <details>. The open state, the keyboard and the accessible name are the element's. Deck restyles the summary, replaces the marker with a chevron, and animates the height using ::details-content plus the interpolate-size opt-in in 02-reset.css — the first time a disclosure could animate to auto height without JavaScript. Give the details elements a shared name attribute for one-at-a-time.
Button rows that go full width when cramped

A block of prose the reader is meant to stop and read. The tone is a three-pixel border-inline-start, so it moves to the right edge under dir="rtl" with no second rule. Deck sets no ARIA role: role="alert" on a message that is present at page load interrupts a screen reader before it has read anything.
Something failed, or is about to.
The explanatory line. min-inline-size: 0 so a long unbroken string cannot push the alert wider than its container.
Confirmation that something worked.
Something the reader should know before continuing.
The first line of an alert. A weight change, not a heading — if it belongs in the document outline, put this class on a real h2-h4.
A consequence the reader should understand first.
Put .anchor on the trigger and --anchor on both trigger and panel. Each pair needs a unique name, so generate it server-side in Keel: <button class="anchor" style="--anchor:--menu-<?= $id ?>">

Header, content, footer in a 100dvh grid whose middle row takes the remaining height — the sticky footer, without the hacks. dvh rather than vh so it tracks a phone browser hiding its chrome. It expects exactly three children.
A round box holding an image or initials. --size drives the width, the height and the font size together, so a size variant is one declaration and the initials can never overflow the circle.
56px.
32px.
A square avatar, for anything that is not a person — an organisation, a project, a repository.
Overlapping avatars. The offset is a fraction of --size, so it stays proportional at every size, and the ring is the surface colour, which is wrong on any other background.
80px.
24px.

A link, not a button. #top is a real target at the head of the document, so the browser moves focus there along with the scroll. A button calling scrollTo() leaves a keyboard user parked at the bottom of the page while looking at the top of it, which is the whole bug this component usually ships with. Showing and hiding is a scroll-driven animation, so there is no scroll listener anywhere -- same mechanism as .scroll-progress in 16-motion. visibility is in the keyframe on purpose: it takes the link out of the tab order and out of the accessibility tree while it is off screen, which is what aria-hidden reaches for and which CSS can actually do by itself. deck.js only steps in where…
A small inline status pill. Sized in em, so it tracks whatever text it sits next to rather than needing a size variant per context.
Failed, overdue, rejected.
Brand tint. For a label that names a category rather than a status.
Adds a leading dot in currentColor, so it takes the tone's text colour without a second class. The dot is decoration — never ship one with no text beside it, because colour alone is not a status.
Paid, shipped, passing, active.
Filled with the brand colour. The highest-emphasis badge; use one per view or it stops meaning anything.
Pending, expiring: needs attention, nothing is broken.
An announcement strip. Top or bottom, dismissible, out of the way.

Looks like a link, behaves like a button. Only for a real <button> that has to sit in a row of links — on an anchor it adds a touch target, a ring offset and nowrap to something that wanted none of them.
Brand-coloured border, transparent fill.
The one important action in a view. Solid brand fill; use exactly one per screen so it keeps meaning something.
A fully rounded button, usually paired with .btn-icon.
The 34px size. Still clears the 44px touch target, because the target is a pseudo-element rather than the box.
Tinted, low weight. Good for an action repeated down a list.
The message body. Its corner radii are logical, which is what lets the grouping flatten the correct side in either writing direction.
Typing indicator
A surface with a border, radius and shadow. It brings no padding of its own — put .card-body inside so the header, body and footer can each own their spacing.
The padded region of a card. A column with a gap, so children stack without margins.
Brand-tinted fill and border, for the one card on a page that is an offer rather than a record.
A card that turns into a horizontal media object once it has the room
A card with no border, shadow or background. Grouping without a box drawn around it.
The top region of a card. A flex row, so a title and a control sit on one line; the divider below it belongs to the header, so a card with no header has no stray line.
The top region of a card. A flex row, so a title and a control sit on one line; the divider below it belongs to the header, so a card with no header has no stray line.
Whole card is the link, but nested links still work

A deeper shadow and no visible border, for a surface that should read as floating above the page.
The heading inside a card. Sized independently of h1-h6 so the same card works at any heading level.
Scroll snap does the work. Arrows and dots are progressive enhancement, so it still swipes correctly with JavaScript switched off.
Previous and next. Hidden on a coarse pointer, where the reader swipes instead — so do not also hide the dots.
Text over a slide. The generous block-start padding is there to give the scrim room to fade — without a background the near-white text sits directly on the image and disappears over anything light.
One slide. flex-basis: 100% by default; .carousel-peek makes it 86% so the next one is partly visible, which is the only persistent cue that the track scrolls once the scrollbar is hidden.
The scroll-snap container holding the slides.
Center a thing with a max width and no side effects

The frame, and the palette. Six series colours are computed by rotating --hue-brand, so charts retheme with the rest of the app and stay in one family. That also makes them hard to tell apart for a colour-blind reader — label the marks directly rather than relying on hue.
Area charts read better with a gradient falling off to nothing.
The filled part of a horizontal bar, sized from --value. It grows from the starting edge, which needs transform-origin — a physical property — flipped for RTL in 19-logical.css.
The value printed beside a bar rather than inside it. Prefer this over text on the fill: contrast-color() raises the floor for text on a series colour but does not guarantee AA.

A column. Its height is calc(var(--value) * 1%), so rendering a chart is writing numbers into style attributes. data-label and data-value are drawn as generated content, which means they are for sighted readers only.
Stacked columns: nest segments inside a .chart-col-stack

x: background: repeating-linear-gradient(to top, var(--chart-grid) 0 1px, transparent 1px calc((100% - 22px) / 4))

classes.d: Grouped columns
A grid of --cols columns whose cells mix the series colour with the sunken background by --value, interpolated in oklab.
The key. Built from real buttons it gets a working toggle state for free, because the faded style keys off [aria-pressed="false"].

Conversation view. Consecutive messages from one side group together and only the last one in a run gets the tail.
Composer pinned to the bottom
A centred date pill between days. Styling, not structure — a screen reader hears ordinary text.
A checkbox or radio and its text, laid out as a row that clears the 44px touch target. Wrap the text in .check-text to add a second line.
Card-style choice, good for pricing and plan pickers

classes.d: Horizontal group that wraps instead of overflowing on a phone

First item to one end, last to the other. Beware of combining it with wrapping: each line is justified separately, so a lone item on the second line jumps to the far end and looks stranded. .bar with .push is the predictable version.
Centres the row.
Packs the row against the end edge, which follows the writing direction rather than always being the right.
Kept as the readable name for step 2, which is what most clusters want

A filtering select. It wraps a real <select> that stays in the DOM and stays in sync, so an ordinary form post works with no server-side handling, server-side rendering is just marking options selected, and without JavaScript the reader still gets a working control.
Tell the engine that a component's layout cannot affect anything outside it. On a dashboard with twenty cards this is the difference between one layout pass and twenty.
Centres content and caps it at --container, with the responsive page gutter already applied. Nest one inside another and the inner one adds a second gutter, so use .container-full instead.
Keeps the page gutter, drops the max width. This is what to nest inside another container — a second .container would apply the gutter twice.
The same 76rem as the bare .container, named. Use it when a page should say which width it means rather than rely on the default.
An article with a rail, or a form.
A single column of prose: about 70 characters at the body size, which is inside the maximum line length WCAG recommends.
A wide dashboard or a data grid.

The behaviour hangs off [data-deck-copy], not off .copy-btn. The class is the look and nothing else, so a button with the class and no attribute looks exactly right and does nothing at all -- the single most common way to get this component wrong. Whether a successful copy raises a toast depends on what is inside the button: a .copy-done element swaps in place and no toast fires; without one, deck-extras.js toasts instead. .copy-inline never toasts.
Inline icon-only variant, for an order number or an API key in a table
A horizontal scroller where the off-center items rotate away. Uses scroll snap for the mechanics and 3D only for the read.
Container queries: components respond to their slot, not the viewport

Query a custom property rather than a size. Set --tone on a container and everything inside it adapts, with no extra classes on the children. Supported in current Chrome and Safari; the fallback is simply no change.
Six faces for a rotating status block or an empty-state illustration.

The trigger for a date picker: an input with a calendar icon inside its starting edge and a clear button at the end. The input is readonly and cursor: pointer, because the value comes from the calendar — which also means a reader who knows the date cannot type it.

The calendar panel: a native popover, anchored to its field by 25-anchor.css with the same fallback chain as a menu. Where there is no room below it opens upward, and position-try-order: most-block-size picks the direction with the most room rather than the first that fits — which matters more for a calendar than for a menu.
Whole sections below the fold. Cheap and safe on any page.

A real table with a frozen header and pinned columns. Use it when the reader operates on data — sorts, selects, scans — rather than reads it; .table is lighter for presentation. Must sit inside .dg-wrap, which carries the scroll container and every custom property these rules read.

Below a breakpoint, restacks each row into a labelled card, taking the column name from data-label on the cell. Costs the column alignment that makes a grid comparable; prefer .dg-cq, which asks the container rather than the viewport.
56px rows, for a grid with two lines of content per cell.
34px rows and smaller text, for scanning many rows at once.
The row that holds an empty state, with its height and padding released so the state can be any size.
Column resize grip. deck.js writes the width to the th.
Selection bar that slides in once rows are checked

contain-intrinsic-size is the placeholder height for a skipped row. Get it roughly right and the scrollbar is stable; the `auto` keyword makes the browser remember the real height once a row has been rendered once.

The shadow only appears once the grid is actually scrolled sideways. A box-shadow offset is physical, so the geometry lives here and 19-logical mirrors it for RTL once, rather than once per branch below.
Zebra is opt-in, and it never fights the pinned column background

Sometimes a value has one true direction regardless of the page. An order number, an account number, a URL, and a code block read left to right even on an Arabic page. Isolate them so they do not scramble the text around them.
A conic gradient driven by --value, with .donut-center holding a figure in the hole. One element, no SVG. Give it role="img" and a label — the shape carries the meaning and nothing else conveys it.

classes.d: A side panel. The bottom sheet is in 08-mobile; this one comes in from an edge and is the right shape for filters, settings, and a mobile nav.
The scrolling region. overscroll-behavior: contain stops a scroll that reaches the end from chaining to the page behind.
Pins the drawer to the ending edge instead of the starting one. The inset is logical and mirrors for free; the translate is not, which is why this rule declares its own.
The action row, pinned to the bottom. Pads for the home indicator with max(--space-4, safe-area-inset-bottom).
The title row. Pads for a notch with max(--space-4, safe-area-inset-top).
The drawer's heading. Point aria-labelledby at it.
A toolbar over a contenteditable region. Deck styles the chrome; deck.js wires the commands. The content area inherits .prose, so what you type looks the way it will look when it is published.
The editable region. Its placeholder comes from data-placeholder through :empty::before, so it needs no element and no script to hide it.

The character count. .is-over turns it red past data-limit — a soft limit, since silently refusing keystrokes reads as a broken keyboard. The server has to enforce it, and role="status" makes it audible.

The tool row. Pressed state is [aria-pressed="true"], which deck-extras.js rewrites from queryCommandState after every command and selection change, so the toolbar reflects the caret rather than the last button pressed.
Pins the emoji font stack and metrics so an emoji renders at the same size and baseline on Windows, iOS and Android instead of jumping between them.

One-shot, on load. Use for content that appears, not for every section.
A validation message below a control. Lightened for dark mode with light-dark(), and aligned to flex-start so an icon stays on the first line of a two-line message.
Real height:auto transitions, no measuring in JS. Needs interpolate-size, which tokens opts into on :root.

classes.d: One form control and everything attached to it: label, input, help text, error. The vertical gap between them comes from here, so a field never needs margins.
Two fields side by side on anything wider than a phone
Form fields that pair up inside their own container, not the viewport. This is the one that keeps biting people: a two-up field row inside a narrow modal should stay stacked even on a desktop.
A bordered group of controls that answer one question. Its legend is the group's accessible name, which is what a radio group needs and what a .label above one does not provide.

A dashed drop zone wrapping a real file input. The input is 1px and transparent rather than display: none, so it keeps its place in the tab order, and :focus-within is what makes that focus visible. Deck styles the zone; dropping needs a handler of your own.
Two faces, one footprint. Front and back are stacked in the same grid cell so the card is exactly as tall as its taller side.

Two things about the markup that this file cannot enforce and that fail silently when they are wrong: 1. The label must come AFTER the control. Every lift selector below is `~ label`, and the general sibling combinator only looks forward. Label first and it simply never moves. 2. The control needs placeholder=" " (one space). Without a placeholder attribute :placeholder-shown never matches, so the label sits lifted over an empty field. FINDINGS 61: .float.is-invalid only colours the label. .field.is-invalid in 06-forms.css also reddens the control's border; there is no equivalent rule here, so the same class name does two different amounts of work depending on which wrapper it is on.…
Outlined variant, where the label sits in a notch in the border
A real component rather than the demo's ad-hoc one.
Sticky save bar for long forms on mobile
Pins the action row to the bottom of the viewport with a blur behind it and a safe-area inset for the home indicator. Add matching bottom padding to the form, or the last field sits underneath it.
Semibold. The weight for a label or a name that needs to lead without becoming a heading.

Auto-fitting grid: no breakpoints needed, it responds to its own width

Two-ish columns: an auto-fit grid with a 24rem floor. Identical in effect to .grid-wide, but it writes grid-template-columns directly rather than setting --min, so --min cannot adjust it afterwards. Prefer .grid-wide.

Exactly two equal columns at every width, including a phone. Only for a count that is part of the meaning — a 2x2 comparison. It does not reflow, so it does not satisfy the reflow criterion on its own.
Exactly three equal columns at every width. See .grid-fixed-2.
Exactly four equal columns at every width. On a phone that is four 70px columns; reach for .grid with a --min instead.
Narrows the auto-fit column floor to 12rem, so the grid packs more columns in before it wraps.
Widens the auto-fit column floor to 24rem, so the grid packs fewer, wider columns before it wraps. For cards with a paragraph in them.
A hint below a control. Needs aria-describedby on the control to reach a screen reader — sitting next to it is not an association.
An SVG icon sized in em, so it scales with the text it sits beside and lands on the baseline. Icons are filled with currentColor and inherit the surrounding colour.
A 1.6em icon, for icon tiles and empty states where the default would look undersized.

Small icons reference the heavier cut of the sprite, not a thicker stroke: the symbols are filled outlines, so stroke-width does nothing to them. Every icon ships twice, #name at wght 400 and #name-sm at wght 500, and .icon-sm goes with the -sm symbol. CSS cannot rewrite a <use href>, so the pairing lives in the markup: <svg class="icon icon-sm"><use href="deck-icons.svg#check-sm"></use></svg>
Icon in a tinted tile — for feature rows and empty states
Status dots, counts on an icon, and unread markers.
Marks a field invalid from your own validation, producing the same border and ring as :user-invalid without needing the browser to agree. One of the few states an author writes by hand.

A prefix, suffix or attached button joined to a control. The group takes over the border, radius and shadow, and the input inside strips its own, so the seam does not double up. :focus-within puts the ring around the whole assembly.
A hero block. Kept deliberately plain so the content carries it.
The obvious thing to build once you have drag and drop. An issue queue by status is the same shape as a board.
The scrolling card region, with a 5rem floor so an empty column is still something you can drop onto.
One card. .kanban-card-title is styling, not a heading — if the card opens something, make the title a link.
One column: a fixed width with a viewport cap so a phone still shows a sliver of the next, capped in height by --kanban-height.
Shown in an empty column and hidden by :has(.kanban-card) as soon as one arrives, so nothing has to remember to toggle it.
The column title and count, outside the scrolling area so they stay visible while cards scroll.
The label for a control. A flex row, so a "required" or "optional" marker sits beside the text without extra markup.
A placeholder that holds the space so nothing shifts, and fades the image in once it decodes. Set the aspect ratio on the frame and the layout is stable before a byte arrives.
Generic content placeholder while a region streams in
A blurred low-res preview underneath, if you have one

x: transition: translate var(--dur-2) var(--ease-out), box-shadow var(--dur-2) var(--ease-out)

classes.d: A bordered, clipped column of rows. Use it when the reader reads one row at a time; if they compare values down a column, that is a table.
A group heading inside a list. Styling only: a screen reader hears ordinary text, so if the grouping is meaningful use a real heading.

One row. min-block-size: var(--tap) puts every row at the touch target, and the colour and text-decoration resets mean the row can be an <a> directly — one element, one tab stop, the whole row clickable.
For a status strip: recalls, open campaigns, parts on backorder.

Two implementations. Columns is universal and good for photos where the reading order down each column is fine. Grid masonry is the real thing and preserves row order; it is used automatically where supported.
A wide panel under a nav item. Built on the popover attribute, so escape and outside-click are the browser's job.

A dropdown built on the native popover attribute: light dismiss, Escape, the top layer and one-at-a-time behaviour all come from the platform. 25-anchor.css positions it against its trigger with anchor positioning and a fallback chain, so it flips when there is no room below.

One row in a menu. Works on a button or an anchor — colour and text-decoration are reset so a link needs no help. Hover and focus share a style, so a keyboard user sees what a mouse user sees. 40px tall, which is under the 44px target: a deliberate density trade for a list of eight.
A destructive item. Red is not announced, so the label has to say what it does and a confirmation should stand behind it.
A small heading above a group of items. Styling only — a screen reader hears ordinary text.
A dropdown that should match the width of the field it belongs to
A one-pixel divider between groups of items.
List rows that reveal their metadata as space allows
Same seven steps as every other spacing family: 0 1 2 3 4 6 8.

The short physical-looking names in the utility layer (.mt-4, .px-3) are already logical underneath — .mt-4 sets margin-block-start. These are the explicitly named versions for when the distinction matters in review.

A native <dialog>. Open it with showModal(), never show() and never the open attribute: only showModal() gives the top layer, the backdrop, the focus trap and an inert background. The open and close animate because display and overlay are in the transition with allow-discrete, which is what keeps the element rendered long enough to fade out.
The scrolling region. The modal caps at min(85dvh, 48rem) and clips, so a long body scrolls while the header and footer stay put — which is what keeps the actions above the fold.

The action row, end-aligned. Below 32rem it becomes column-reverse with full-width buttons, so the primary action — last in the markup — is on top where a thumb reaches it, without changing DOM order.
The title row. A flex row aligned to flex-start, so a long title and a close button line up on the first line.
The dialog's heading. Give it an id and point aria-labelledby at it, or the dialog is announced with no name.

One message row. .msg-out flips it to the other edge and reverses the row so the avatar swaps sides. The incoming/outgoing distinction is position and colour only, so name the sender in text for anyone not seeing it.
One destination in a .navbar. Carries the hover and current-page states; use .btn only for actions, never for navigation.
x: transition: background-color var(--dur-1) var(--ease-out), color var(--dur-1) var(--ease-out)

classes.d: Native spinners are tiny and inconsistent across browsers. These are real buttons that clear the touch target.
Tabular figures, so numbers line up in a column and do not jitter when they change.
The scale is 0 1 2 3 4 6 8, declared in 04-layout.css. Every family below implements all seven, so a step that exists anywhere exists everywhere.
True 3D parallax: layers sit at different Z depths inside a perspective container, so the browser does the math on the compositor. No scroll handler, no jank.
Country select welded to the number. The number stays LTR even in an RTL document, because a phone number always reads left to right.
Ping ring for a live indicator — a dot with a halo going out
A richer tooltip: a heading, body copy, and actions. Used for the "what does this labor code mean" pattern.
The action row at the bottom of a popover card. A button here can close the panel with popovertargetaction="hide" and no script.
The explanatory text inside a popover card.
The heading inside a popover card.
Repeat a header on every page of a long report
Hidden on screen, shown on paper

Three ways to say "something is happening", and the choice is only ever about one thing: whether you know how much is left. .progress and .ring do, .spinner does not. There is no standalone meter -- a bar drawn from a value rather than from an element is .chart-meter, in 14-charts.css. .progress goes on a real <progress>, so the element carries the value, the maximum and the role. The two vendor pseudo-elements have to be written as separate rules: a vendor pseudo-element in a shared selector invalidates the whole rule for the other engine. Same constraint as .range.
Prose: for anything that came out of a WYSIWYG or markdown
Pushes this element and everything after it to the far end of a flex row. The one-class replacement for a spacer div.
deck.js renders the modules into this frame. Kept square, with a quiet zone, so it stays scannable at any size.
Radius on the leading and trailing edges, not left and right

A slider. The track and thumb are vendor pseudo-elements with different names and different box models per engine, so every declaration is written twice — WebKit needs a negative block-start margin to centre the thumb and Firefox does not.
Two stacked native range inputs. Real inputs mean real keyboard support and a real form post; the track between them is drawn from --lo and --hi.
The current value of a slider. Put it on an <output>, which is an implicit live region, so the value is announced as the slider moves.
Ticks under a single or paired range

The inputs are written HIGHEST value first -- 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 -- and row-reverse draws them 1 to 5. That is not a quirk, it is the whole mechanism: to light a star and everything below it, the selector has to reach forward from the chosen one, and CSS has no previous-sibling combinator. Reversing the row turns "everything below" into "everything after". Get the order wrong and it fails recognisably: the stars fill from the wrong end and the posted value is the mirror of the one clicked. :focus-visible + label uses the ADJACENT sibling, so each label must come immediately after its own input.
Read-only display: a fill percentage rather than whole stars
Aspect boxes for media
Reaction pill, like a Slack or Teams reaction

A conic gradient for the fill, a radial mask for the hole. Three custom properties shape it: --value, --size, --thickness. The mask is the thing to understand. It applies to this element AND its whole subtree, so a label centred inside a .ring is punched out along with the middle -- it renders, it takes up space, it is in the accessibility tree, and it is invisible. That is what .ring-wrap and .ring-label below exist for: an unmasked wrapper that stacks the label over the ring as a sibling rather than a child. FINDINGS 60: place-items and the three font declarations here are the fossil of the approach that does not work. They style a child nobody can see -- .ring-label repeats all three on…
Ripple. deck.js sets --rx/--ry from the pointer position.
Series 1. Every chart mark reads --series, so a colour is set once on the element and the fill, stroke and legend swatch all follow.
A scene establishes the vanishing point. Children need preserve-3d to stay in the same space instead of being flattened.
A progress bar that fills as the page scrolls — good for long reports
Everything stays on one line and scrolls sideways — cards, chips, dates
A control with an icon inside its starting edge. The icon is pointer-events: none, so clicking it focuses the field underneath rather than doing nothing.
Vertical page rhythm: a block of --space-section, which is a clamp that grows with the viewport. For spacing inside a component reach for .stack instead.

A one-of-N control: equal-width children in a sunken track with the selected one raised. Styled from [aria-selected="true"] or .is-active. Built from radio inputs it needs no JavaScript and gets arrow keys free — but Deck does not style :has(:checked), so that version needs one rule of your own.
Marks a field invalid from your own validation, producing the same border and ring as :user-invalid without needing the browser to agree. One of the few states an author writes by hand.
<dialog class="sheet"> on a phone, a centred modal from 40rem up.
The scrolling region. Pads for the home indicator, and contains its overscroll so reaching the end does not scroll the page behind.
The drag handle at the top of a bottom sheet. Deck draws it and does not implement the drag — swiping down does nothing — so always ship a real close button as well.
The title row of a sheet.
The sheet's heading. Point aria-labelledby at it.
Sticky header that condenses once you scroll past the top
A tiny inline chart for a table cell or a stat block.
A FAB that fans out into related actions.

x: transition: opacity var(--dur-2) var(--ease-out), translate var(--dur-2) var(--ease-spring), scale var(--dur-2) var(--ease-spring)

classes.d: Exempt from the reduced-motion reset in 02-reset.css: instead of freezing it slows to 2.4s. A frozen spinner reads as a hung page, which is worse for everyone than a slow one. Note border-block-start-color rather than border-top-color -- the lit segment starts at the block start in any writing mode.
Content + rail. Collapses to one column below the width it needs.

Puts the rail on the starting edge without touching markup order, so the main column stays first for a screen reader and for the keyboard. Use it for supplementary navigation; not for a rail holding the first thing a reader needs.
Vertical rhythm without margin collapse surprises
No gap. For two elements that must touch.
A hairline. A label and the control it names, when the two read as one thing.
Tight vertical rhythm, for a label and its control or a title and its subtitle.
The default rhythm for related blocks inside a card or a section.
The default, named. Same as .stack with no step class.
Loose vertical rhythm, for separating whole sections of a page.
Very loose, for whole sections of a page where .section is too much.

Past twelve everything holds the last step rather than snapping back to zero. Without sibling-index() that is as far as CSS can count. .pile in 21-space3d.css has the same fallback and is MISSING this line, so its ninth card stacks on top of the first.
A stat block that stacks tight, then spreads, then goes inline
Live status line: dot plus label, the pattern used in status pages
A wizard. The timeline in 07 records what happened; this one shows where you are in a process you are actively moving through.
Horizontal where there is room, vertical below a breakpoint. Prefer this over .stepper-vertical: four steps with notes do not fit across a phone, and a horizontal stepper that squashes is unreadable.
Vertical on a phone, where five steps side by side never fits

A sticky header. Where scroll-state container queries are supported the blur and shadow live on an ::after that is transparent until the header actually sticks, so in flow it looks like part of the page. The treatment rides on a pseudo-element because a scroll-state container can style its descendants but not itself.
Underline that draws in from the start edge

An on/off control that takes effect immediately, drawn over a real checkbox. If the reader has to press Save afterwards, use .check instead. Add role="switch" when "on"/"off" reads better than "checked"/"unchecked".

One trigger. Styled from [aria-selected="true"], so the visual state and the accessible state are the same attribute and cannot disagree. The unselected state carries the same transparent border, so selecting one changes a colour and never moves anything.
A real table, kept a table at every width, because values in a column are only comparable while the columns exist.
Tighter cell padding, for a table the reader scans rather than reads.

Below 40rem, restacks each row into labelled lines, taking the label from data-label on the cell. Every cell needs one. The thead is clipped rather than removed, so header association survives; print undoes the whole thing, because paper is never narrow.

The scroll container for a table, and not optional. It carries the border, radius, background and overflow-x, without which a wide table pushes the whole page sideways. Add tabindex="0" when the table overflows, or a keyboard user cannot scroll it.

The strip. Scrolls sideways rather than wrapping, because tabs that wrap stop reading as a strip. Deck styles the tabs and ships no keyboard behaviour: if you use role="tablist" you must add the roving tabindex and the arrow keys yourself, or the role promises what the page does not do.
Secondary text colour. Still meets contrast against every surface Deck defines, so it is safe for body copy rather than decoration only.
One step down the type scale, for secondary text and dense rows.
Grows with its content instead of scrolling in a 4-row box
A rotated column header that still measures and aligns correctly
deck.js writes --tilt-x and --tilt-y from the pointer position. Both are registered angles, so they interpolate smoothly back to rest.
x: transition: rotate var(--dur-3) var(--ease-out), scale var(--dur-2) var(--ease-out)

classes.d: The ::after tooltip could never flip. This one can, and it can carry a real arrow that stays pointed at the anchor.
The arrow on a .tip. background: inherit takes the tip's colour, and justify-self: anchor-center keeps it pointed at the trigger whichever way the tip has flipped.

One notification. The accent colour is a single custom property, --toast-accent, which paints the edge, the icon and the timer together, so a kind is one declaration. Built by Deck.toast() rather than written by hand; touch-action: pan-y lets a horizontal swipe dismiss it while a vertical drag still scrolls the page.

A CSS-only tooltip: the text comes from data-tip through ::after, so there is no second element. It cannot flip near a window edge, cannot escape an overflow:hidden ancestor, and is hidden entirely on a coarse pointer. Never put anything essential in it, and pair it with aria-label — generated content is not a reliable accessible name.

x: transition: background-color var(--dur-1) var(--ease-out), border-color var(--dur-1) var(--ease-out), color var(--dur-1) var(--ease-out), fill var(--dur-1) var(--ease-out), stroke var(--dur-1) var(--ease-out)
transition: translate var(--dur-2) var(--ease-out), scale var(--dur-2) var(--ease-out), rotate var(--dur-2) var(--ease-out)
transition: inline-size var(--dur-3) var(--ease-out), block-size var(--dur-3) var(--ease-out)

classes.d: A responsive frame for a native video or an embed, plus styling for the native controls where the browser allows it.
Poster overlay with a play button, for a click-to-load embed
Any long stack of cards: an activity feed, a chat log, search results

Elements that persist across the navigation. Give the same view-transition-name to the matching element on both pages and the browser tweens between them — a row in a list morphing into a detail header.
A count or dot anchored to a corner of something
Vertical text for a table header that would otherwise need a 40 character column, or for a sidebar label.
Lift an element toward the viewer inside a scene, rather than faking it with a bigger shadow.
